family: level machine with a binary counter (nested drain/copy)
summary: Works in levels: a block (10111)^b is moved word by word to the left end, drained, and recycled as the next block, 2 to 6.6 times as long. For the four short tails the level map is exact (b' = (9b+c)/2 with the next tail chosen by b mod 4; proved visit by visit in Lean, composed symbolically for all b). Other levels count in binary between the blocks, and the next level then depends on the digits. No growth cycle; no halt in 5.6e15 steps (12 levels); open.
title: What is known about 1RB0RE_0LC0RF_1LD1LC_1RA0LD_0RD1RE_---0LB
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RE_0LC0RF_1LD1LC_1RA0LD_0RD1RE_---0LB.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The run is a sequence of levels, each about 2 to 6.6 times as long as the one before. Every single visit of the left end in the common phases is a Lean theorem for all block sizes, and for the four common level types the map from one level to the next is an exact formula. But some levels contain a binary counter, and what follows them depends on the binary digits of a block length; no closed description of those levels has been found. The machine halts exactly when the head, in state A, stands on a 0 followed by 1 0; that has not happened in 5.6·1015 steps.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 5.6·10<sup>15</sup> steps
claims.text: An exact accelerated simulator (blocks of 30 cells, run-length coded; a repeated cycle is skipped only after it has been re-run with the counts as free variables) runs 5,608,376,993,382,856 steps without a halt. Its tape was compared with plain step-by-step simulation at 50,000,050,596 steps: same state, all 399,483 cells equal. The shared C simulator tools/c/triage.c independently runs 109 steps (52,423 cells visited, 28,979 ones).

claims.title: Growth shape: sqrt/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.46). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.615).

claims.title: Exact halting condition
claims.text: The machine halts exactly when a configuration A> 0 1 0 occurs: state A on a 0 whose right neighbours are 1 then 0. (F is entered only from B reading 1; if F reads 1 it steps back onto the 0 that B wrote. So only B reading 1 followed by 0 halts, and B gets there from A reading 0.) A hand argument from the table, not in Lean.

claims.title: Grow phase, one visit
claims.text: 0^∞ D>0 0 1^5 (00111)^a (100)^(a+1) (10111)^(b+1) R reaches 0^∞ D>0 0 1^5 (00111)^(a+1) (100)^(a+2) (10111)^b R in 28a + 55 steps, for every a, b and every tape R further right.

claims.title: 120 one-visit rules for the other phases
claims.text: Each visit of the left end in the phases of the four common level types is a theorem for every block size: entering the drain phase (tails P, Q, R, S), the 14-visit drain cycle that removes four words 100, the four endings according to the block length mod 4 up to the recycling of the left block, and the pour phase of tail S. Each rule is one visit: from one tape with the head at the left end to the next.

claims.title: The rules cover whole levels; the level map for b = 12..27
claims.text: Plain simulation of 64 levels (tails P, Q, R, S, b from 12 to 27): every visit is an instance of one of the Lean rules, and the next level is the one the formulas give: for tail P, b' = (9b+10)/2, (9b+11)/2, (9b+10)/2, (9b+9)/2 with next tail P, Q, R, S for b = 0, 1, 2, 3 mod 4; for Q the constants are 12, 13, 12, 11; for R, b' = b+4; for S, b' = 2b+3 or 2b+4.

claims.title: The level map for every b (12 of 14 level types)
claims.text: A symbolic run with the block counts as free variables, which stores a cycle only after re-running it with free counts and splits into cases by remainder when a jump needs it, follows a level from start to the next level start. For 12 of the 14 level types that occur, every case ends in a level start of one of the 14 types (91 cases), with the next block length a linear form such as 18k+113 from 4k+24. The check fails for the two types that contain the binary counter (2 cases), so the set is not closed. Python, not checked by Lean.

claims.title: A binary counter inside some levels
claims.text: In a level whose tail is (100111)^m the tape between the blocks is a string of the words 100 (digit 0) and 11100 (digit 1). Read as a binary number it goes up by one each time the tail loses one word, from 0 to m−1 (six runs, m up to 100). The next level depends on the digits of m: for b = 400 and m = 1..69 the next block length lies between 1,205 and 2,657 and the tail takes nine shapes.

claims.title: No level start that was tried halts
claims.text: About 25,000 random level starts of the 14 types (block counts 20 to 149) all reach a level start of one of the same 14 types; so do the counter levels with b = 400, m = 1..69; random level starts with counts below 20 (many more shapes) do not halt either. Scratch scripts, plain simulation.

claims.title: Twelve levels of the real run
claims.text: Level starts from blank tape: b = 13, 77, 83, 670, 674, 5,397, 10,798, 62,092, 279,420, 1,257,395, 5,658,282, 11,316,567 (the last at step 1.92·10<sup>15</sup>), each step agreeing with the level map where the map is known. No configuration returns with only one or two counts grown, so there is no growth cycle to prove.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. A proof that it runs for ever needs a closed description of the counter levels: a set of tapes with an arbitrary string of the two digit words between the blocks. Nothing suggests a halt.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows yet. This machine works in levels: it moves a long block of the tape to the left one word at a time, drains what it built, and starts again with a block 2 to 6.6 times as long. Most levels follow an exact formula; some contain a binary counter and are not understood.

facts.text: One visit of the left end in each phase, proved in Lean for every block size.
No halt in an exact accelerated simulation, checked cell by cell against plain simulation at 5·10<sup>10</sup>.
Level types whose next level is computed for every block length.
Levels with a binary counter inside: no closed description.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.46). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.615).
After 109 steps the tape spans 52,423 cells (33,516 left of the start, 6,210 right), with a density of 1s of 0.553.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: When it would halt
html: The machine has one halting instruction: state F reading a 0. F is reached only from state B reading a 1, and B then leaves a 0 behind and moves right. If F finds a 1 it steps back onto that 0, and nothing happens. So the machine stops only if B finds a 1 with a 0 right after it, and B gets to such a place only from state A reading a 0.
It halts exactly when the head, in state A, is on a 0 and the next two cells are 1 and 0.
In the whole run so far the head in state A on a 0 has always found either another 0 or two 1s to its right.

sections.heading: Visits and levels
html: Look at the tape only at the moments when the head reaches a new cell at the far left. It then reads
0 0 1^5 (00111)^a · X

where (00111)^a means the word 00111 written a times. Between two such moments the head sweeps to the right and comes back: one visit. A visit adds one word 00111 at the left and changes the rest X in a way that does not depend on a.
Now and then a visit rewrites the whole left block as (10111)^a. The tape is then
0 0 1^5 100 (10111)^b · tail

and a new level starts. A level is described by the block length b and the short tail after the block. During a level the block is moved to the left one word per visit (the grow phase), then the pile of words 100 that this leaves is removed four words per 14 visits (the drain phase), and the left block is recycled.

sections.eyebrow: From one level to the next
sections.heading: The level map
html: Four short tails keep coming back; call them P = 100 1111 0 1111 00 111, Q = 100 1111 0 1111 0 111, R = 100 1111 0 11111 0 111, S = 100 1111 0 1111 00 1. For P and Q the next level is given by the remainder of b when divided by 4:

tailb = 4kb = 4k+1b = 4k+2b = 4k+3
P(9b+10)/2, tail P(9b+11)/2, tail Q(9b+10)/2, tail R(9b+9)/2, tail S
Q(9b+12)/2, tail P(9b+13)/2, tail Q(9b+12)/2, tail R(9b+11)/2, tail S

So such a level multiplies the block by 4.5, and the remainder mod 4 picks the next tail, as in a Collatz-type problem. Tail R gives b+4 and leaves a second long block on the tape; tail S doubles b and leaves a block of six-cell words whose length m is about b/2.

These formulas are checked in two ways: by plain simulation for b = 12 to 27, where every visit is an instance of a Lean rule, and by a symbolic run with b as a free variable (a Python program, not Lean) for every b.

sections.heading: A binary counter between the blocks
html: After a level with tail S the tape carries a block (100111)^m. In the next level the machine does something new. Between the pile of words 100 and that block a string of two kinds of words appears: 100 and 11100. Read 100 as the digit 0 and 11100 as the digit 1: the string is a number in binary. Each time the block at the right loses one word, the number goes up by one:
1000 → 1001 → 1010 → 1011 → 1100 → …

until the block is used up and the number is m−1. Then the digits are consumed from the right, and how the level ends depends on them. With b = 400 and m from 1 to 69, the next block length takes values from 1,205 to 2,657 and the next tail nine different shapes, in no order that we can see.

This is why the method that settles similar machines does not finish here. That method lists finitely many tape shapes with free block lengths and shows that each leads to another in the list. A counter passes through a different shape for every value, so a proof needs a different kind of invariant: a set of tapes that allows any string of the two digit words in the middle.

No level start that was tried halts: all remainders for the common tails, about 25,000 random level starts, and the counter levels with small m. The evidence points to a machine that runs for ever, but it is evidence, not a proof.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.
